analysis.one_liner: Bans insurers from retroactively canceling coverage immediately and orders reinstatement for people already dropped.
analysis.headline: The House never acted on the bill; it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee from July 15, 2010 until the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the new health care law, insurers are barred from rescinding—that is, retroactively canceling—a person's coverage. But that ban does not take effect right away. This bill would make it effective immediately and go a step further: any insurer that dropped someone between the law's enactment and this bill's passage would have to put that person back on the plan and pay for care received in the meantime. It would not fine insurers for those drops during the gap period.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose health coverage was rescinded after the new health care law passed. Rescission is the practice of an insurer selling a policy, then canceling it retroactively—often after the person files a costly claim or reveals a pre-existing condition—leaving the patient with huge medical bills. The bill would force reinstatement and payment of those claims, and would move up the start of the general ban on rescissions so no one else could be dropped under the old rules in the meantime.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose coverage was retroactively canceled

how_it_helps.text: Requires any insurer that rescinded coverage between March 23, 2010 and the bill's enactment to reinstate the enrollee and treat their claims as if the rescission never happened [S2] [S3].
Makes the health care law's prohibition on rescissions take effect on the day this bill is enacted, rather than on the law's standard delayed schedule [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, who would have to reinstate customers they had dropped, pay for claims they had refused, and absorb the cost of an immediate nationwide rescission ban. The bill does soften this by exempting insurers from any penalty for rescissions that occurred during the gap period.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets insurers off without any penalty for rescissions during the gap period, so an insurer that wrongly dropped a sick patient during that window would have to pay the claim but face no fine [S2] [S3].

The practical gain is limited: the health care law's consumer protections, including the rescission ban, were already on track to apply to plan years beginning roughly six months after enactment, so the bill mainly helps a narrow window of people dropped in 2010.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people dropped from coverage in 2010, the bill offered real relief: reinstatement and paid claims. The cost falls on insurers, though the penalty exemption is a genuine concession—an honest supporter would have to acknowledge that insurers who dropped sick patients during the gap period would face no punishment beyond paying what they owed. The bill's narrow scope reflects that it was a gap-filler rather than a major reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 15, 2010 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; the action history shows no further steps [S5].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill was never reported out of committee or scheduled for a vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are better off because the bill died: no expedited rescission ban, no reinstatement orders, and rescissions during the interim period carried no consequences under existing law. Consumers dropped from coverage in that window got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, who faced no new rules

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan lineup appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would force insurers to reinstate people they had dropped and pay their claims, and would start the rescission ban immediately—cutting into a practice insurers used to avoid paying for expensive patients. But it also waives any penalty for rescissions during the gap period, softening the hit. Rescinding coverage of costly enrollees is a practice that directly conflicts with patients' interest in keeping their coverage.
